description: Team VNK is three high school students from Minnesota focused on computer science, health science, and machine learning. We aim to build practical software grounded in real research and engineering constraints. We are here to test our skills against real-world constraints and build something genuinely useful from the ground up.
summary:
VNK-HEMS (VNK Health Evaluation & Mission Support) is a full-stack astronaut health monitoring platform built with a React/TypeScript frontend and a Java/Spring Boot/MongoDB backend. The software enables crew members to independently log physiological, behavioral, and visual biomarkers (ranging from cardiovascular vitals and body mass to mood and OCT retinal scans) and evaluates them against pre-flight baselines and clinical thresholds.

VNK-HEMS maps 15 core measurements across all 21 NASA Human Research Program (HRP) spaceflight risks and five primary space hazards. It empowers non-physician astronauts to self-assess through color-coded risk scores (1–100), interactive body-area visuals, dynamic trend charts, plain-language exam instructions, and automated daily, weekly, and monthly check-in reminders.

As missions extend to the Moon and Mars, communication delays and isolation limit real-time ground support. VNK-HEMS bridges this gap by providing actionable triage guidance, streak-based engagement, and clear escalation protocols to detect health anomalies early and protect crew readiness.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The process follows a structured workflow:

  • Multi-Modal Data Logging: Crew members independently log physiological, behavioral, and visual biomarkers, ranging from cardiovascular vitals and body mass to mood, white blood cell counts, and image-based scans (OCT/fundus).
  • Baseline & Threshold Evaluation: The backend processes incoming readings against pre-flight baselines and clinical thresholds, converting them into percentage changes or absolute deviations.
  • Rule-Based Risk Scoring: A deterministic, rule-based scoring engine evaluates each measurement against abnormal and dangerous ranges, mapping 15 core measurements across all 21 NASA HRP spaceflight risks and five primary space hazards.
  • Interactive Triage & Guidance: The React frontend visualizes status via color-coded risk scores (0–100), interactive body-area figures, dynamic trend charts, and plain-language exam instructions with step-by-step guidance.
  • Escalation & Monitoring: Automated daily, weekly, and monthly check-in reminders track compliance, while escalation protocols provide clear guidance for alerting the Crew Medical Officer or flight surgeons.

What benefits does it have?

  • Protects crew health by detecting early anomalies in critical areas such as cardiovascular adaptation, bone and muscle fitness, immune dysregulation, and Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).
  • Bridges communication delays and isolation during deep-space transit to the Moon and Mars by providing offline-capable triage guidance and structured escalation pathways.
  • Enhances crew adherence through streak-based engagement, automated reminders, and intuitive visual tools designed for non-physician astronauts under high-stress conditions.

What is the intended impact of the project?

As human spaceflight extends beyond Low Earth Orbit toward the Moon and Mars, communication delays (ranging from minutes to over 20 minutes one-way) and deep-space isolation severely limit real-time support from ground flight surgeons.

Our intended impact is to bridge this gap by empowering astronauts to act as autonomous first responders to their own health. By providing early anomaly detection, continuous longitudinal trend tracking, and structured escalation protocols, the platform protects crew readiness, mitigates long-term spaceflight risks (such as Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome and bone demineralization), and ensures mission success across prolonged deep-space transit.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Languages: Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL
  • Backend & API: Java 25, Spring Boot 4 (Jackson 3), MongoDB 7, Docker Compose, Gradle wrapper
  • Frontend & UI: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, TailwindCSS, Shadcn/UI, Radix UI Components, TanStack Query, Recharts, React Router v6
  • Data Processing & Storage: Jackson JSON processing, MongoDB document repositories, Cloudinary (image storage)
  • Development & Infrastructure: Visual Studio Code, Git, Node.js, npm/yarn, Vercel (Frontend deployment), GitHub Cloud
  • Data Sources & Standards: NASA Human Research Program (HRP) risk evidence, NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), NASA OCHMO Technical Briefs, CDC NHANES datasets

How is your project creative?

  • Instead of just typing notes, astronauts can log daily numbers, check-ins, and even medical images (like eye scans for vision health) all in one place.
  • Our project takes complex NASA medical research and turns it into simple, automated scoring rules that work completely offline without needing an internet connection.
  • We designed it with streaks, reminders, and an interactive body map to make health check-ins fast, engaging, and easy to use even when astronauts are tired or stressed.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Delayed Signals: The app had to work entirely on local devices during deep-space signal blackouts when Earth support isn't available.
  • Feasibility for Non-Doctors: Astronauts aren't all medical specialists, so the design needed clear risk scores and plain-language instructions that anyone can follow quickly.
  • Accurate NASA Research: Every single metric, warning rule, and health threshold is strictly based on actual NASA research and known spaceflight risks.
  • Technology Constraints: We used a reliable, modern tech stack (React and Java Spring Boot) to ensure the app is fast, organized, and secure.
